summary: John Henry Piet was a scholar in Indology, religious studies, and philosophy who studied at Hope College, Western Theological Seminary, Hartford Seminary, Princeton Theological Seminary, and Columbia University. He served as Professor of English Bible and Mission at Western Theological Seminary (1960–1984).

John Henry Wright was a scholar of history, archaeology, and linguistics who studied at Dartmouth College and the University of Leipzig under Georg Curtius. He held professorships at Ohio State (1873–1876), Dartmouth (1878–1886), Johns Hopkins (1886), and Harvard University (~1887–1908).

John Herbert Harington was an Indologist and historian who served at The Asiatic Society as secretary in 1790 and president from 1825 to 1828. He was also President of the Council of Fort William College (~1801–1819).

John Hick worked in philosophy and religious studies. He held posts at Cornell, Princeton Theological Seminary, Cambridge, Birmingham, and Claremont Graduate University (attested 1985–1989), succeeding Ninian Smart.
John Hope studied at the University of Edinburgh (~1740–1750), where he later held an academic post from approximately 1761 to 1786.

John Hurrell Crook, a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, studied at Southampton, Cambridge under Robert Hinde and William Homan Thorpe, and with Sheng Yen. He taught at the University of Bristol (~1963–1995) and founded the Western Chan Fellowship in 1997.

John Irwin worked in history, archaeology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. He served as Assistant Keeper (1945) and Keeper (1959–1978) at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and was a visiting professor of Indian art history at the University of Michigan (1985).

John J. Holder, a scholar of philosophy and Buddhist studies, studied under Harry Krebs. He held a visiting research post at the University of Oxford and taught at St. Norbert College (attested 2006, 2018).

John J. Makransky, working in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and philosophy, earned his PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison under Geshe Lhundup Sopa. In 1992, he became Assistant Professor of Comparative Theology and Buddhist Studies at Boston College.

John James Jones was a scholar in Indology and Buddhist studies who earned his M.A. at Aberystwyth University (1911–1914). He served at the National Library of Wales as Assistant Keeper (1926) and Deputy-Keeper (1928).

John Jorgensen works in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology. He has held positions at Griffith University, the Australian National University, and La Trobe University's China Studies Research Centre (attested 2019).

John Kieschnick is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology. He held a post at the University of Bristol (~2005–2011) before joining Stanford University around 2011 as Robert H. N. Ho Family Foundation Professor of Buddhist Studies.

John Lane Bell is a philosopher who completed his D.Phil. at Oxford (1977–1980). He held posts at the London School of Economics (~1968–1989), the University of Western Ontario (~1989), and Cambridge (2001).

John Leyden was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Edinburgh, St Andrews, and under Henry Thomas Colebrooke. He was Professor of Hindustani at Fort William College (1806) and served as secretary at The Asiatic Society (~1806–1811).

John Lockwood Kipling was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He taught at Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy School of Art (1865), served as Principal of the National College of Arts (1875–1893), and curated the Lahore Museum (1875–1893).

John M. Koller is a scholar of philosophy, Indology, and religious studies who studied at the East-West Center under Shri Krishna Saksena, Charles Alexander Moore, and George T. Artola. He served as professor of philosophy at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (attested 1988, 1999).

John M. Rosenfield, a scholar of history, archaeology, and Japanology, completed his PhD at Harvard under Benjamin Rowland. He was a professor at Harvard (1965–1991) and served as Curator of Oriental Art at the Harvard Art Museums (~1971–1991).

John Marshall, a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology, studied at Cambridge and the British School at Athens under Arthur Evans. He served as Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1931) and was a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge (~1927–1958).

John McKenzie was an Indologist and philosopher who studied at Aberdeen, New College, Edinburgh, and Tübingen. He served at Wilson College, Mumbai, as Professor (1908) and Principal (1921–1944), and was Vice-Chancellor of the University of Mumbai (1931–1933).

John McKerrell was a scholar of linguistics and Indology who served in the Madras Civil Service as Translator of Telugu and Kannaḍa (1804) and held an ex officio post at the College of Fort St. George.
